messages.subject: CIM & Epistatic mapping
parts:
Hi karl,
Can you give me a detailed description on how to perform a Composite
Interval Mapping in R/qtl? I am not good at the use of "additive
covariate".
How to perform a epistatic qtl mapping, if the single effects of the
two qtl are not significant but their joint effect is. In other words,
is it possible to find epistatic interactions between two loci (not
qtls) in R/qtl, like EPISTACY or EPISTAT do?
And, how to select the threshold for epistatic QTL mapping, by
jiontLOD, interactionLOD, or others?

Many thanks!
Dong

messages.author: ab8dbe3bec292afe
messages.subject: Re: CIM & Epistatic mapping
parts:
To do composite interval mapping, you need to pull out the genotype
data for a particular marker,
and include it is an additive covariate in scanone. In an
intercross, you'll need to create a
matrix with two columns, coding the additive and dominance effects of
the marker. If there are
missing genotype data, you'll need to impute the missing genotypes at
the marker, which can be
done using the function fill.geno(), or use the functions sim.geno()
and scanqtl() to do this via
multiple imputation.

For the analysis of epistatic QTLs, you can get at QTLs that have an
important interaction but
no main effect by using scantwo() to do a two-dimensional, two-QTL scan.

How to select thresholds for such 2-d, two-QTL scans has not yet been
fully resolved. The results
of a permutation test with scantwo() might be of use, but I'm not
prepared to provide a recipe.

regards,
karl

messages.author: 5523cb16ec47d553
messages.subject: Re: CIM & Epistatic mapping
parts:
Hi Dong,

To pull out the genotype data for a cross object called "mycross", use
the pull.geno command in R/qtl:

markerdata <-pull.geno(mycross)
E4M8a <- markerdata[,"E4M8a"]

which should work as long as your marker is labeled "E4M8a". In
general, you can access columns of a matrix by their column names,
using the syntax mymatrix[,"mycolumn"].

Hope this helps!
ani

messages.author: ab8dbe3bec292afe
messages.subject: Re: CIM & Epistatic mapping
parts:
Dear Dong,

You have those pretty much right, though argmax.geno() doesn't simulate
the genotypes, but rather calculates the most probable sequence of
underlying
genotypes given the available marker data.

It's possible to export inferred genotypes for use in other software;
likely
fill.geno() is the only one that would be useful for that. If your
dataset
is called "mycross", then the following imputes the missing or partially
informative (or possibly in error) genotypes and copies them over the
observed data:

mycross <- fill.geno(mycross)

You can then use write.cross() to write the data back to a file.
There are
mapmaker ("mm") and QTL Cartographer formats ("qtlcart"). I've not
tested
this function all that much.

If your genotype data, consisting mostly of dominant markers, are not
very
informative (try looking at plot.info(mycross) to see how much
information
is missing), you could be severely misled by the above approach, as
you'd be
inferring the underlying truth, and then pretending that those
inferred genotypes
were precisely the truth. Important uncertainty would not be taken
into account.
I think your best bet is to stick with analysis via scanone(), scantwo
(),
or fitqtl(), using either EM or imputation to take account of that
uncertainty.

karl
